analysis.one_liner: Caps US prescription drug prices at the lowest price charged in 11 other wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in committee for 18 months, attracted zero cosponsors, and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Health and Human Services Secretary to set a yearly maximum price for every prescription drug, based on the lowest retail price for that drug among 11 reference countries including Japan, Germany, France, Canada, and the UK. Those caps would apply to Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA care, federal employee insurance, and Indian Health Service programs. It would also require drug makers to sell at that price to uninsured people and people with private insurance, and fine manufacturers five times the amount they overcharged federal programs, with the money going to NIH for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in every major federal health program, plus uninsured and privately insured Americans, who would pay no more for a drug than the lowest price charged in peer countries. Federal and state governments would also save billions on Medicare and Medicaid drug spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare, Medicaid, VA patients and the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: HHS must set an annual reference price for each drug at the lowest retail list price among Japan, Germany, the UK, France, Italy, Canada, Australia, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, and Sweden, when pricing data exists for at least three of them [S3].
The caps apply across Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA hospital and medical care, the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program, and Indian Health Service programs [S3].

Drug makers would have to sell at the reference price to everyone, including people without insurance and people with private coverage, so the price ceiling reaches the whole market, not just federal programs [S3].

Manufacturers that charge above the cap owe a civil penalty of five times the amount they overcharged federal health programs, and those penalty dollars are transferred to the NIH for drug research and development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose US prices are typically far higher than prices in other developed countries, would lose revenue. Lower prices could also mean less money available for future drug research and development.

drawbacks.text: Tying US prices to the lowest price in any of 11 peer countries goes further than the approaches used in most peer countries themselves, which set national prices through their own health systems rather than importing the cheapest foreign price [S3].

A hard cap set at the lowest foreign price, with a civil penalty for charging above it, could shrink the revenue drug companies expect in the US market, which critics of international reference pricing argue would reduce investment in developing new medicines [S3].

When pricing data is not available in at least three reference countries, the Secretary would set the price through judgment calls about a drug's value and development costs, which invites disputes over how those factors are weighed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients and taxpayers the upside is large: the bill targets the core reason Americans pay several times what people in peer countries pay for the same drugs, and it extends the cap to the uninsured and privately insured rather than only to federal programs. The honest cost is that sharply lower US prices could mean slower development of future drugs, and the penalty structure leaves drug companies little room to charge more for a genuinely breakthrough medicine. Weighing that tradeoff was exactly what committee review was for; it never happened.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to six House committees and then a health subcommittee, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Debbie Dingell introduced the bill on June 20, 2023, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee plus the Ways and Means, Armed Services, Veterans' Affairs, Oversight, and Natural Resources committees [S1][S5].
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor; the cosponsor list stayed at zero for the life of the bill [S4].
The bill was referred to a Health subcommittee in June 2023, July 2023, and again in December 2024, but no subcommittee or committee ever took it up, and it never reached the House floor [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without any vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: US drug prices stayed as they were, and no committee ever weighed the case for capping them at international levels.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The only recorded sponsor was a Democrat, and no Republican and no other Democrat signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill died with support from a single member of one party [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill caps their US prices at the lowest price charged in 11 peer countries across Medicare, Medicaid, and other federal programs, and extends that cap to the uninsured and privately insured, directly cutting revenue from the world's highest drug prices. Its death left current pricing untouched.

The bill's price caps also apply to generic drugs and biologics, so low-cost generic makers would face ceilings too, though most generics already sell near the lowest international price. Patients who buy generics would generally see little change.

industries.industry: Health insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Private plans would pay no more than the reference price for covered drugs, lowering their drug costs. That saving would flow to premiums and cost-sharing only if insurers passed it on, which the bill's cap on what plan coverage plus cost-sharing can exceed encourages but does not fully guarantee.
